werk/pharoah-sanders-wisdom-through-musi.text:
Wisdom Through Music by the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders was released in 1973 on Impulse! Records. It was recorded in New York and Los Angeles and produced by the drummer Lee Young, the younger brother of the saxophonist Lester Young. Also playing on the record are flautist James Branch, pianist Joe Bonner, bassist Cecil McBee, drummer Norman Connors and three percussionists.

AllMusic praises the exuberance of High Life, the raw and soulful Love Is Everywhere and the festive joy of Selflessness. Other critics are more critical. According to All About Jazz, percussion and strong rhythms keep the music down to earth, but the sound is somewhat muddy and the bells and vocals sometimes sound dated. PopMatters calls Wisdom Through Music and The Golden Lamp the pieces that save the record, thanks to their restraint and beautiful melodies.
werk/pharoah-sanders-wisdom-through-musi.listen: Listen to High Life and notice the rolling, festive drumming and the vocals, which together define the mood of the track.

werk/phil-spector-be-my-baby.text: What the writers dreamed up in New York was often recorded elsewhere. In Los Angeles, the producer Phil Spector worked with a fixed group of session musicians, later called the Wrecking Crew. He stacked guitars, pianos, strings and echo into a wall of sound. Be My Baby by The Ronettes from the summer of 1963, written with Ellie Greenwich and Jeff Barry, is the textbook example. The producer became a star.
werk/phil-spector-be-my-baby.listen: Hal Blaine's drum intro, three dull beats and a hard crack, is one of the most copied ever. Then the wall opens up.

werk/pinar-toprak-the-wind-gods.text:
The Wind Gods is the music for the documentary The Wind Gods: 33rd America's Cup, a film about the 2010 America's Cup, the sailing contest between Oracle Team USA and the Swiss Alinghi. The film was made by Skydance Productions, directed by Fritz Mitchell and narrated by Jeremy Irons. In 2013 it was shown on the American broadcaster PBS.

Pinar Toprak wrote the music. The soundtrack album was released on Caldera Records and contains eighteen music tracks and one commentary fragment. Many titles follow the story of the film, such as First Race 1851, The Final Race and The America's Cup Is America's Again. The film score won the International Film Music Critics Association award for best documentary score in 2011.
werk/pinar-toprak-the-wind-gods.listen: Listen to The Final Race and try to hear how the music attempts to translate the tension of a sailing race.

werk/pink-floyd-a-saucerful-of-secrets.text:
A Saucerful of Secrets is Pink Floyd's second studio album, released on 28 June 1968. Recording began in August 1967 at EMI Studios in London, with producer Norman Smith. Syd Barrett was functioning ever more poorly, so David Gilmour was brought in, and Barrett left before the album was finished. Whereas Barrett had been the main writer on the debut, each member now contributed songs and vocals.

Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun is the only track on which all five members play. Corporal Clegg is the band's first song about war. Jugband Blues is often seen as a reference to Barrett's departure. The album reached number nine in England. The reviews were mostly positive, although many critics found it weaker than the debut.
werk/pink-floyd-a-saucerful-of-secrets.listen: In Jugband Blues, listen to the Salvation Army brass band that Norman Smith arranged on Syd Barrett's advice.

werk/pink-floyd-animals.text:
Animals was released on 21 January 1977 and was Pink Floyd's tenth studio album. The band recorded it in 1976 at their own studio, Britannia Row in London, which they had just converted. The album continues the long tracks of Meddle and Wish You Were Here. Roger Waters wrote almost everything, with only Dogs written together with David Gilmour. Sheep and Dogs went back to pieces that the band had already played live.

It is a concept album about society in Britain in the mid-1970s, loosely based on George Orwell's Animal Farm. The lyrics divide people into dogs, pigs and sheep. Pigs on the Wing opens and closes the album. The cover shows an inflatable pig between the chimneys of Battersea Power Station. No singles were released, and the first reviews were mixed, but the album was later more highly valued.
werk/pink-floyd-animals.listen: Listen to Dogs and notice how the track builds over a long span.

werk/pink-floyd-atom-heart-mother.text:
Atom Heart Mother was released on 2 October 1970 and was recorded at EMI Studios, now Abbey Road, in London. Pink Floyd began it after the music for the film Zabriskie Point had ended in discord in Rome. The title suite, which takes up the whole of the first side, came about from instrumental ideas arising from rehearsals. Ron Geesin wrote the arrangements for orchestra and choir, with the band mainly playing the accompaniment. Side two offers three songs by Waters, Wright and Gilmour and ends with Alan's Psychedelic Breakfast.

It was the band's first album to reach number 1 in England. The cover, with a cow, shows no title and no name. The reviews were mixed, and the band members themselves were later negative about it.
werk/pink-floyd-atom-heart-mother.listen: Listen to Alan's Psychedelic Breakfast and notice the sounds of breakfast between the musical sections.

werk/pink-floyd-meddle.text:
At the beginning of 1971 Pink Floyd had no fixed material and no clear idea of where the album should go. The band worked between gigs, from January to August, at EMI Studios, now Abbey Road, and at smaller studios such as AIR and Morgan, which could handle 16 tracks. To get going, the group devised experiments: each member played separately on his own track, without hearing what the rest were doing. From those trials, known as Nothings, the track Echoes eventually grew.

Meddle is regarded as a transitional record between the group of Syd Barrett and the era led by Roger Waters. The record sounds more cohesive than its predecessor Atom Heart Mother. One of These Days is largely instrumental and revolves around a bass line that David Gilmour ran through a Binson Echorec. Then comes A Pillow of Winds, one of the band's few quiet acoustic love songs. Critics were positive and the record did well in England.
werk/pink-floyd-meddle.listen: Listen to One of These Days and notice the pulsing bass line with which the track begins and how it builds up.

werk/pink-floyd-obscured-by-clouds.text:
Obscured by Clouds is the soundtrack to the French film La Vallée by Barbet Schroeder. Pink Floyd recorded the music in France in 1972, in two sessions during a busy touring period, while the group was already working on The Dark Side of the Moon. The tracks are short and concise, unlike the long instrumental pieces of other records. Several tracks show a country influence, mainly through the acoustic guitar, and Wright uses the VCS 3 synthesizer.

Free Four, written by Roger Waters and about the death of his father in the war, was the only single. The album reached number six in England. Critics and fans are divided.
werk/pink-floyd-obscured-by-clouds.listen: Listen to Free Four and notice the acoustic rhythm guitar and the counted-in start.

werk/pink-floyd-the-dark-side-of-the-moo.text:
After a tour in 1971, Roger Waters proposed making an album about what drives people mad: the pressure of band life and the mental problems of Syd Barrett, the former band member. The songs were first played live and took shape during performances. Recording took place in two sessions in 1972 and 1973 at EMI Studios in London. Pink Floyd used multitrack recording, tape loops and analogue synthesizers. Engineer Alan Parsons brought in the session singer Clare Torry for The Great Gig in the Sky.

The album deals with conflict, greed, time, death and mental illness. Between the tracks, fragments of conversations with the crew and philosophical quotations are heard. Money and Us and Them were released as singles. The cover with a prism is by Storm Thorgerson. Critics reacted enthusiastically and the album often appears on lists of the greatest albums ever.
werk/pink-floyd-the-dark-side-of-the-moo.listen: In The Great Gig in the Sky, listen to Clare Torry's voice. Notice how her wordless singing carries the emotion.

werk/pink-floyd-the-piper-at-the-gates-o.text:
The band became known through performances at the UFO Club in London and through the singles Arnold Layne and See Emily Play. Recording of the debut took place from February to May 1967 at EMI Studios on Abbey Road, under producer Norman Smith. EMI gave the band complete freedom. In the studio next door, The Beatles were working on Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. Syd Barrett wrote almost all the songs. The music mixes long improvisations with short pop songs and a playful take on psychedelia, with plenty of reverb and echo. During the recording Barrett became increasingly confused through LSD, and a year later he left the band.

The title comes from the children's book The Wind in the Willows. Astronomy Domine and Interstellar Overdrive remained staples of the live shows for a long time. The album reached number six in Great Britain and is regarded as an important psychedelic album.
werk/pink-floyd-the-piper-at-the-gates-o.listen: In Interstellar Overdrive, listen to the long improvisation and the studio effects. Notice how freely the band handles sound.

werk/pink-floyd-ummagumma.text:
Ummagumma is a double album by Pink Floyd, recorded partly live and partly in the studio and released on 7 November 1969 by Harvest Records. The first disc contains live recordings from Mothers Club in Birmingham and the College of Commerce in Manchester.

On the second disc each band member gets half a side for a work of his own, without contributions from the others. Richard Wright made Sysyphus, Roger Waters Grantchester Meadows, David Gilmour The Narrow Way and Nick Mason The Grand Vizier's Garden Party. The studio recordings ran from September 1968 to July 1969. The album was well received at the time and reached the British top five, but critics and band have viewed it less favourably since.
werk/pink-floyd-ummagumma.listen: In Grantchester Meadows, listen to the calm acoustic sound, which refers to Roger Waters's youth in the suburbs of Cambridge.

werk/pink-floyd-wish-you-were-here.text:
After the success of The Dark Side of the Moon the band members were exhausted and found it hard to come up with new material. Between January and July 1975 they worked on the follow-up at EMI Studios in London. Three songs they had played on tour in 1974 served as the starting point. Roger Waters wanted to split Shine On You Crazy Diamond and place two new songs between the parts, and he got his way.

The record is about longing, alienation and criticism of the music industry. Shine On You Crazy Diamond is a tribute to Syd Barrett, who had left the group seven years earlier. During the final mix he unexpectedly walked into the studio. Welcome to the Machine and Have a Cigar target the record business, and synthesizers are combined with acoustic guitar. The first reviews were mixed, but later the album was regarded as one of the best of the 1970s.
werk/pink-floyd-wish-you-were-here.listen: Listen to the beginning of Shine On You Crazy Diamond, Pts. 1-5, and notice the four-note guitar phrase that carries the rest of the track.

werk/pixies-doolittle.text:
After Surfer Rosa in 1988, the band toured Europe and were enthusiastically received there. They had already played songs for the second album on John Peel's radio programme. For Doolittle the label 4AD chose Gil Norton as producer. Recording began on 31 October 1988 at Downtown Recorders in Boston, with a budget of 40,000 dollars, four times as much as for the debut. Norton set to work on short, raw songs, slowing some down and letting others run longer. He refined the sound with compression and reverb on the guitars.

Black Francis wrote lyrics with surreal imagery, biblical violence and torture. The album is known for the interplay between quiet verses with Kim Deal's bass and loud, distorted guitars. Kurt Cobain said that Smells Like Teen Spirit was strongly influenced by that sound. Melody Maker and Sounds named it album of the year.
werk/pixies-doolittle.listen: In Debaser, listen to the difference between the soft and the loud parts. Notice the bass and the distorted guitars.

werk/pixies-head-carrier.text:
Head Carrier was released on 30 September 2016 and is the sixth album by the Pixies. It was recorded at RAK Studios in London under producer Tom Dalgety, who replaced Gil Norton, the man behind the previous four albums. Bassist Paz Lenchantin had joined in 2014 for the tour around Indie Cindy and plays here for the first time as a full member. She succeeded Kim Deal, who had left in 2013. The title refers to a cephalophore, a saint who carries his own head, in this case Saint Denis of Paris.

Production began in late 2015. Um Chagga Lagga was the first single, Talent the second. Lenchantin co-wrote All I Think About Now and sings it herself. The song is about Kim Deal and takes the form of a thank-you letter. NPR streamed the whole album online from 22 September.
werk/pixies-head-carrier.listen: Listen to All I Think About Now and notice how Paz Lenchantin's different voice carries this song about Kim Deal.

werk/pixies-indie-cindy.text:
Indie Cindy was released on 19 April 2014. It was the Pixies' first album since Trompe le Monde in 1991 and the first without bassist Kim Deal. Simon Ding Archer, formerly of The Fall, took over the bass. The record gathers the tracks from the three EPs EP1, EP2 and EP3 from 2013 and 2014. These had been recorded in 2012 under producer Gil Norton, who had also made Doolittle, Bossanova and Trompe le Monde.

In the United States the album reached number 23 on the Billboard 200, the band's highest position there. Critics were divided. Many found it more predictable than the older work and compared it to a Black Francis solo record, because Deal was missing. NME was positive and heard in Bagboy a free, adventurous and explosive sound. The Telegraph felt that the band had found gritty melodies within the bigger, smoother style of Trompe le Monde.
werk/pixies-indie-cindy.listen: Listen to Bagboy, picked out by NME as a highlight, and judge for yourself whether it sounds free, adventurous and explosive.

werk/pixies-surfer-rosa.text:
Surfer Rosa is Pixies' debut album and came out in March 1988 on the British label 4AD. After the mini-album Come On Pilgrim, label boss Ivo Watts-Russell wanted a full-length record. Steve Albini became the producer. In December 1987 the band recorded in ten working days at Q Division in Boston, on a modest budget of ten thousand dollars. Albini refused royalties, because he considered them an insult to the band.

Albini placed the guitar amplifiers in a tiled bathroom and used room microphones for an open, pounding drum sound. The lyrics contain Spanish, references to Puerto Rico and shocking subjects such as mutilation and incest. Gigantic became the only single. The album did not reach the charts, but often appears on lists of the best rock albums. Billy Corgan and PJ Harvey cite it as an inspiration, and it influenced Nirvana's In Utero, which Albini also produced.
werk/pixies-surfer-rosa.listen: Listen to Something Against You and notice the raw singing voice, which Albini ran through a guitar amplifier.

werk/pixies-trompe-le-monde.text:
The band recorded this fourth album in Burbank, Paris and London, with producer Gil Norton. It was Pixies' last record before the band split up two years later, and the last with founder and bassist Kim Deal. The title comes from the opening track and means Fool the World. It is a pun on trompe-l'oeil, the painting technique with which a painter makes the viewer believe that painted objects are real.

The sound leans towards heavier, metal-like guitars, especially in Planet of Sound, Trompe le Monde, Space (I Believe In) and Subbacultcha. Head On is a cover of The Jesus and Mary Chain and became a single. U-Mass is about the university where Black Francis and Joey Santiago met. One reviewer later wrote that Kim Deal had a smaller role and that the album was almost a Black Francis solo record.
werk/pixies-trompe-le-monde.listen: In Head On, listen to the way the band shapes a song by The Jesus and Mary Chain into its own sound.

werk/porter-wagoner-sing-duets.text:
Porter Wagoner and Skeeter Davis Sing Duets was released in May 1962 on RCA Victor. Both already had a successful solo career in country music and were signed to the same label. For this album they worked together for the first time. Chet Atkins produced the sessions, which took place in Nashville in February 1962.

The record contains twelve duets, mostly covers of existing country songs. Rock-A-Bye Boogie comes from the Davis Sisters, the group of which Davis had previously been a member. There are also Have I Told You Lately That I Love You, Gonna Find Me a Bluebird and A Little Bitty Tear. In June 1962 Billboard chose the album as Spotlight Album of the Week and praised the traditional country sound with strings.
werk/porter-wagoner-sing-duets.listen: Listen to Have I Told You Lately That I Love You and notice how the two voices sound together.

werk/portishead-dummy.text:
Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons met in 1991 during a course for aspiring entrepreneurs. They recorded their first ideas in Neneh Cherry's kitchen, then at Coach House Studios in Bristol. Guitarist Adrian Utley joined and brought a cimbalom and theremin. The album was created with techniques from hip hop: sampling, scratching and making loops. The group recorded their own music onto vinyl, ruined it by walking on it and sampled from that again, so that the sound is old and crackly.

Dummy was released in August 1994 as a debut. It sounds darker and stranger than the label trip hop suggests: sparse beats, a cinematic atmosphere and Gibbons's sad voice. Sour Times and Glory Box became the best-known tracks. The record received glowing reviews, won the Mercury Music Prize in 1995 and strengthened Bristol's reputation as the capital of trip hop.
werk/portishead-dummy.listen: Listen to Glory Box and notice how Gibbons sings above a slow, crackly beat. Hear how much space remains between the sounds.

werk/primal-scream-sonic-flower-groove.text:
This debut album was released on 5 October 1987 on Elevation Records. At first the band worked for four weeks with producer Stephen Street, but the sessions were abandoned because they did not like the result. The ensemble then made a fresh start in London with Mayo Thompson of Red Krayola as producer. By the time the record was finished, it had cost 100,000 pounds.

The music is psychedelic, Byrds-like jangle pop. It is the only Primal Scream album with founder Jim Beattie, who appears on the cover as Jim Navajo. The reception was mixed. One reviewer called the record a real gem, another found it nothing more than fluff. The album reached number 62 on the British chart, but performed modestly for a major record company. That disappointment was an important reason why the original band broke up shortly afterwards.
werk/primal-scream-sonic-flower-groove.listen: Listen to Gentle Tuesday, the track that impressed Melody Maker. Notice the jangly guitar work and the gentle psychedelic mood.

werk/primal-scream-vanishing-point.text:
Vanishing Point is Primal Scream's fifth studio album and was released on 7 July 1997 on Creation Records. The record is named after the 1971 film, and Kowalski is intended as an alternative soundtrack to it. Singer Bobby Gillespie called it a speed-freak road-movie record. Everything was written and recorded in two months using two portable eight-track studios in the rehearsal room in Chalk Farm, and mixed over another month. Much of it arose from live improvisation, over which sounds, loops and vocals were later layered. It was the first album with bassist Gary Mani Mounfield, formerly of the Stone Roses.

The music draws on dub, ambient, dance and krautrock, and on bands such as Motörhead, Can and the Stooges. In Motorhead, Gillespie sang the first verse through a Darth Vader mask. Augustus Pablo, Glen Matlock and the Memphis Horns played as guests. Critics saw the record as a return to form. It reached number 2 on the British chart.
werk/primal-scream-vanishing-point.listen: Listen to Kowalski and think about how this track fits a film full of paranoia and speed, for which it was intended as an alternative soundtrack.

werk/primal-scream-xtrmntr.text:
XTRMNTR, an abbreviation of Exterminator without vowels, is Primal Scream's sixth studio album and was released on 31 January 2000 on Creation Records. It was the last full-length album on that label. Whereas earlier records had been more hedonistic, the band now took a political stance and attacked the government, the police and multinationals. Gary Mani Mounfield shared in the songwriting for the first time. Kevin Shields of My Bloody Valentine helped with production and playing, and Bernard Sumner of New Order also contributed.

The sound is more aggressive than before, with raw electronic sounds that recall industrial. Accelerator became the last single on Creation. The press reacted very enthusiastically: Metacritic reached an average of 90, NME and Uncut placed the record at number 2 of 2000, and NME gave it the award for best album in 2001. In 2019 The Guardian placed it at number 65 of the best albums of this century.
werk/primal-scream-xtrmntr.listen: Listen to Accelerator and notice the raw, electronic sounds on which the track rests.

werk/prince-buster-i-feel-the-spirit.text:
I Feel the Spirit is Prince Buster's debut album from 1963. Blue Beat Records released it in Great Britain, and it was the first ska album to be released outside Jamaica. All twelve tracks are his own. The Drumbago All Stars, the Les Dawson Blues Unit and the Rico Rodriguez Blues Band provided the backing.

The best-known tracks include Madness, They Got to Come, Wash Your Troubles Away and Black Head Chinaman. The song Madness was covered in 1979 by the British ska group Madness, who made a single of it and put it on the album One Step Beyond. The cover photo is by Dezo Hoffmann.
werk/prince-buster-i-feel-the-spirit.listen: Listen to Madness and notice how the ska beat carries the track.

werk/prince-controversy.text:
Controversy is Prince's fourth album, released on 14 October 1981 on Warner Bros. He wrote and produced everything himself, bar one track, and played most of the instruments. It is the first record on which he is strongly associated with the colour purple and the first with striking spelling in the titles.

The title song asks questions about his origins and sexuality and includes the Lord's Prayer as a vocal piece. Ronnie, Talk to Russia is a political appeal to President Reagan. Private Joy is light pop funk and Annie Christian mentions events such as the murders of children in Atlanta and the death of John Lennon. Jack U Off closes as an electronic rockabilly. Rolling Stone found the message refreshingly topical. In 1981 the record came in at number eight in the Pazz & Jop poll.
werk/prince-controversy.listen: Listen to Annie Christian and notice the lyrics, which list a series of news events of the time.

werk/prince-dirty-mind.text:
Dirty Mind by Prince was released on 8 October 1980 on Warner Bros. He recorded the album in May and June in an improvised sixteen-track studio in the basement of his home on Lake Minnetonka. He played almost all the instruments himself and worked as engineer under the pseudonym Jamie Starr. Some of the songs he wrote on tour, when he was playing for Rick James.

The sound is rawer than on his previous records, with funk, new wave, R&B and dance, and more rock rhythms. Even punk rock is heard in Sister. The title song runs on a metronomic disco rhythm. Uptown is about tolerance and When You Were Mine was later recorded by Cyndi Lauper. It is the only record of his without a slow jam. Critics see the album as influential for black pop of the 1980s.
werk/prince-dirty-mind.listen: Listen to Dirty Mind and notice the tight disco rhythm, the falsetto singing and the metallic keyboard melodies.

werk/prince-for-you.text:
For You is Prince's debut album, released by Warner Bros. on 7 April 1978. He wrote, arranged, produced and played everything himself. In September 1977 he began in Minneapolis, after which the project moved to the Record Plant in Sausalito. Producer Tommy Vicari was formally credited, but he was given little say. For the opening track, 46 vocal parts were layered on top of one another.

The album cost three times the original budget, and afterwards he called himself a physical wreck. The lead single Soft and Wet reached number 12 on the soul chart. Robert Christgau found it a lot of skill and little challenge, but appreciated Baby and Soft and Wet. Of his falsetto he wrote that it surpassed Stevie Wonder's.
werk/prince-for-you.listen: Listen to For You, the opening track, and notice the layered vocals.

werk/prince-purple-rain.text:
Purple Rain grew out of a deal with Warner Bros. After the breakthrough with 1999, Prince demanded that the label finance a feature film with himself in the lead role, with new songs as the soundtrack. Recording ran from May 1983 to March 1984. He wrote more than a hundred songs and chose nine that fitted the film. His band the Revolution received a permanent name in 1983 and was expanded with Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman.

The sound is fuller than on earlier records, with layers of guitar, synthesizers and drum machines. Let's Go Crazy and When Doves Cry reached number one on the American Hot 100. When Doves Cry has no bass line. The last three tracks, including the title track, were recorded live in Minneapolis. Critics praised the mix of electronics and ordinary instruments. Darling Nikki led to complaints and contributed to the Parental Advisory stickers.
werk/prince-purple-rain.listen: Listen to When Doves Cry and notice what is missing: there is no bass line, which leaves the drum machine and the vocals extra exposed.

werk/procol-harum-a-salty-dog.text:
This third album by Procol Harum was recorded in March 1969 and came out that same year. It has a nautical theme; the cover resembles the Player's Navy Cut packet. Matthew Fisher produced the album, his first time, and left the band shortly afterwards. It was also the last record with bassist Dave Knights. Musical tensions began to grow between guitarist Robin Trower and the rest of the group, as Crucifiction Lane shows, a track with a rare vocal part by Trower.

The record is more varied than its two predecessors, with rock, blues and pop. The title song is the band's first track with an orchestra, and the piano riff at the beginning was inspired by a train whistle that Gary Brooker heard in Switzerland. The song reached number 44 on the British chart and the album number 27. Rolling Stone found it confusing, Robert Christgau gave it an A+.
werk/procol-harum-a-salty-dog.listen: Listen to A Salty Dog and notice the orchestra, heard for the first time on a record by the band.

werk/procol-harum-broken-barricades.text:
Broken Barricades is the fifth album by the English rock band Procol Harum. It was released in April 1971, in the same week the group began an American tour, and on 11 June 1971 in the United Kingdom. It was the last album on which guitarist Robin Trower played, until The Prodigal Stranger in 1991.

Chris Thomas produced the album. Song for a Dreamer is a tribute by Trower to Jimi Hendrix, whose death in September 1970 had deeply affected him. Trower sings this track himself, as well as Poor Mohammed. The rest is sung by Gary Brooker, who also plays piano. Chris Copping plays bass and organ and B. J. Wilson drums, while Keith Reid wrote the lyrics. The die-cut cover was designed by C.C.S. Associates, with photos of the four musicians from left to right.
werk/procol-harum-broken-barricades.listen: Listen to Song for a Dreamer and notice Robin Trower's own singing in this tribute to Jimi Hendrix.

werk/procol-harum-home.text:
Home is Procol Harum's fourth album, released in 1970. Organist Matthew Fisher and bassist David Knights had left and Chris Copping joined. That brought the group almost back to being the Paramounts of old, and it was meant to bring the R&B back into the sound.

The first recordings in the autumn of 1969 at Trident Studios in London, led by Fisher, were rejected because the band was not satisfied with the sound and the playing. In February 1970 the group began again at Abbey Road with producer Chris Thomas. The cover is a parody of a British snakes and ladders game, with the band members themselves as pieces. The album was released in June 1970, reached number 34 in the United States and number 6 in Denmark. It was preceded by the single Whisky Train, written by Robin Trower with lyricist Keith Reid.
werk/procol-harum-home.listen: Listen to Whisky Train, the single that preceded the album, and notice the timbales heard in it.

werk/procol-harum-shine-on-brightly.text:
After the hits A Whiter Shade of Pale and Homburg, Procol Harum released a second album in September 1968. On paper Denny Cordell produced the record, but halfway through the recording he and the band parted ways, partly because he wanted to place drummer B.J. Wilson with Joe Cocker. Most of the production work was then done by Tony Visconti.

The record is regarded as an early example of progressive rock. The opening track Quite Rightly So is about a broken love. Rambling On tells of a boy who wants to imitate Batman and jumps off a roof. The great closer is In Held 'Twas In I, a suite that takes up almost a whole side and consists of several parts. The single fell short of the first two, but in the United States the album sold better than the debut. Rolling Stone was unfavourable, but AllMusic later called the suite bolder than anything The Nice or The Moody Blues made.
werk/procol-harum-shine-on-brightly.listen: Listen to In Held 'Twas In I and notice how the different parts of the suite flow into one another, right through to the Grande Finale.

werk/public-enemy-apocalypse-91-the-enem.text:
For their fourth album Public Enemy chose a new direction partly out of necessity. According to Hank Shocklee, the discs containing almost all the tracks from four or five years had been stolen, so the group had to re-record in a hurry. The sound therefore became leaner than on earlier records, and live musicians played a bigger role. The album was released in 1991 on Def Jam.

On 1 Million Bottlebags the group protests against the spread of malt liquor in the African-American community. With the metal band Anthrax they made a thrash version of Bring the Noise. The controversial video for By the Time I Get to Arizona showed the murder of Governor Evan Mecham. Can't Truss It became the most successful single. Critics praised the record, and in The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop poll it came in at number 2.
werk/public-enemy-apocalypse-91-the-enem.listen: Listen to Bring The Noise and notice how the metal band Anthrax and the group's rap together make a single track.

werk/public-enemy-fear-of-a-black-planet.text:
Fear of a Black Planet is Public Enemy's third album, released on 10 April 1990 by Def Jam and Columbia. It was produced by the team The Bomb Squad, who further developed the sample fabric of the previous album, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back. The rapper Chuck D wanted to make a deep, complex record. The furore around Professor Griff, who was thrown out of the group after anti-Semitic remarks, played a part in the writing.

The sound consists of intricate collages of shifting rhythms, many samples, fragments from the media and idiosyncratic loops. The lyrics deal with organisation and strength within the black community, social problems and race relations, and criticise institutional racism. The record was a commercial and critical success and sold two million copies in the United States. In 2004 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.
werk/public-enemy-fear-of-a-black-planet.listen: Listen to Fight the Power and notice the layers of samples and sound fragments beneath the rap.

werk/public-enemy-it-takes-a-nation-of-m.text:
After the debut Yo! Bum Rush the Show, Public Enemy wanted to make a record with more pace for their live shows, and at the same time the hip hop equivalent of Marvin Gaye's What's Going On. The group recorded the album in 1987 and 1988 in New York. The recording reportedly cost about 25,000 dollars and took thirty days, thanks to a great deal of preparatory work in their own studio on Long Island. The production team, the Bomb Squad, built a busy, aggressive sound with influences from free jazz, heavy funk and musique concrète, over which the rapper Chuck D laid his political lyrics.

The album was released on 28 June 1988 and received wide praise for its production and lyrics. In The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop poll it was by a wide margin the best album of 1988. Rebel Without a Pause does not run on a sample of Funky Drummer: Flavor Flav played the rhythm on the drum machine throughout the entire track.
werk/public-enemy-it-takes-a-nation-of-m.listen: Listen to Rebel Without a Pause and notice the continuous rhythm that runs throughout. Also hear the scratch near the end of the track, by Terminator X.

werk/public-enemy-muse-sick-n-hour-mess-.text:
The title of Public Enemy's fifth album is an inverted expression: music in our message instead of message in our music. With it the group says that the message is more important than the music. The record came out in August 1994 on Def Jam, in the midst of the gangsta rap era. Critics wondered whether the group was still relevant.

First single Give It Up reached number 33 on the American Hot 100 and remained the group's only top 40 hit in the United States. Reviews were mixed: some found the rhymes and the production weak, others praised the combination of a storm of sound and funk. Sales suffered from Def Jam's move from Sony to PolyGram. Even so, the album went gold in October 1994.
werk/public-enemy-muse-sick-n-hour-mess-.listen: Listen to Give It Up and notice how the groove and Chuck D's voice interlock.

werk/public-enemy-yo-bum-rush-the-show.text:
Yo! Bum Rush the Show is Public Enemy's debut album and was released in March 1987 on Def Jam Recordings. It was recorded at Spectrum City Studios in Hempstead, New York. The record brought together the sample-rich production of the Bomb Squad and the scratching of DJ Terminator X with the black nationalist politics of the rapper Chuck D. As a result it was not well received everywhere by radio and critics.

The music is bare and confrontational: a pounding pulse, hard drums and a high electronic tone, without melody. Most radio programmers ignored the album, but it still became one of the fastest-selling hip hop records. The singles were Public Enemy No. 1 and You're Gonna Get Yours. In the British press it scored high: NME called it the best record of 1987. Later it is regarded as one of the most influential hip hop albums.
werk/public-enemy-yo-bum-rush-the-show.listen: Listen to You're Gonna Get Yours and notice the hard drums and Terminator X's scratches.

werk/queen-a-day-at-the-races.text:
After an exhausting tour for A Night at the Opera, Queen withdrew in the summer of 1976 to make a new album. It was recorded at The Manor, Sarm East and Wessex Sound Studios, for the first time without producer Roy Thomas Baker. The band produced it themselves, with Mike Stone as engineer. The title, like that of the previous record, refers to a Marx Brothers film.

The music is varied. Tie Your Mother Down is blues rock with a slide solo by Brian May. The Millionaire Waltz changes key and time signature, with striking bass work by John Deacon. In Somebody to Love, Freddie Mercury, May and Roger Taylor had their voices recorded over one another so many times that it sounds like a gospel choir of a hundred singers. That track became the biggest hit of the record. In the United Kingdom, Japan and the Netherlands the album topped the charts.
werk/queen-a-day-at-the-races.listen: Listen to Somebody to Love and notice the choir in the choruses: that is just three singers, recorded again and again. Hear how their voices together become one great gospel choir.

werk/queen-a-night-at-the-opera.text:
In 1975 Queen were practically broke, because a contract with Trident left almost all the money they earned with others. That frustration led to Death on Two Legs. After a conflict lasting months the group got free and signed with EMI and Elektra. With producer Roy Thomas Baker the record was made in four months at seven studios, reportedly the most expensive record up to that time.

The production is richly layered, with many stacked voices and guitars. The songs draw on ballads, music hall, sea shanties, Dixieland, hard rock and prog rock, and besides the usual instruments a double bass, harp and ukulele are heard. Bohemian Rhapsody, almost twice as long as an average single of the day, became the first number one in the United Kingdom. The reviews were positive, and the record made the band world-famous.
werk/queen-a-night-at-the-opera.listen: Listen to Bohemian Rhapsody and notice how the band's voices are stacked into a great choir.

werk/queen-another-one-bites-the-dust.text: Another One Bites the Dust by Queen was released in August 1980. Bassist John Deacon wrote the bass riff, inspired by the disco group Chic. On Michael Jackson's advice they released it as a single. The song reached number one in America and was also played on black radio stations. A stadium band had a funk hit, and not every rock fan was happy about that.
werk/queen-another-one-bites-the-dust.listen: The bass riff recalls Good Times by Chic. Also hear the sounds that have been played backwards.

werk/queen-bohemian-rhapsody.text: Bohemian Rhapsody by Queen, from the album A Night at the Opera, was released on 31 October 1975. The song begins as a ballad, moves into an opera section for which the voices were recorded over one another some 180 times, then becomes hard rock and ends quietly. It has no chorus, and it lasts almost six minutes. Even so, it spent nine weeks at number one in England. The video helped usher in the era of the music video.
werk/queen-bohemian-rhapsody.listen: Count the sections: ballad, opera, hard rock, coda. In the opera section, hear how the voices jump from left to right.

werk/queen-jazz.text:
After a hefty tax bill, Queen decided in 1978 to record outside the United Kingdom. Brian May left for Canada in July, while the rest rehearsed in Nice. The band visited the Montreux Jazz Festival, which probably inspired the title, and David Bowie persuaded them to record at Mountain Studios in Montreux. They then worked at Super Bear Studios in France, with Roy Thomas Baker as co-producer. A stage of the Tour de France gave Freddie Mercury the idea for Bicycle Race.

In Mustapha, Mercury sings in a mixture of English, Arabic, Persian and possibly invented words. In Fat Bottomed Girls, guitar and bass are in drop-D, rare for the group. Bicycle Race has a change of time signature from 4/4 to 6/8 and a section in which guitars imitate a bicycle race. The album was released on 10 November 1978 and reached number 2 in the United Kingdom. The shifting styles were both praised and criticised.
werk/queen-jazz.listen: Listen to Bicycle Race and notice the change from 4/4 to 6/8 and the section in which guitars imitate a bicycle race.

werk/queen-news-of-the-world.text:
After their 1977 tour, Queen went into the studio in July for their sixth album, with Mike Stone as co-producer. Only two months had been booked at Sarm East and Wessex Sound Studios in London; the previous record had taken five months. At Wessex the Sex Pistols were also working on their album. Punk had attacked progressive rock groups, and the band responded with a simpler, more rootsy sound, as Brian May put it.

We Will Rock You is deliberately kept simple: stomp, stomp, clap, so that the audience could join in. We Are the Champions became the first single and reached number 2 in the United Kingdom. Sheer Heart Attack is punk rock, Sleeping On The Sidewalk blues rock and Get Down, Make Love funk. The reactions were mixed at first. The album reached number 4 in the United Kingdom and number 3 in the United States.
werk/queen-news-of-the-world.listen: Listen to We Will Rock You and notice how little is needed: stomping and clapping.

werk/queen-sheer-heart-attack.text:
Sheer Heart Attack was released on 8 November 1974 and was Queen's third album. After two albums with progressive themes, the band now chose more pop-oriented songs and more conventional rock. Roy Thomas Baker produced it together with the group. The recording in the summer of 1974 went with difficulty, because Brian May contracted hepatitis after a tour and later developed a duodenal ulcer, after which he ended up in hospital during the sessions. Afterwards he recorded Dear Friends, among other things.

Killer Queen became the first single, reached number 2 in Great Britain and was the band's first American top twenty hit. The album took Queen to the peak of popularity in the United Kingdom and beyond. It was later named by magazines as one of the group's best records.
werk/queen-sheer-heart-attack.listen: Listen to Killer Queen and notice the dense layers of voices and guitars surrounding the singer.

werk/quincy-jones-go-west-man.text:
Go West, Man! is Quincy Jones's second studio album and was released in 1957 on ABC Records. It is a record for a larger ensemble, on which Jones acts as conductor. A group of outstanding jazz musicians play on it, including the trumpeters Conte Candoli, Pete Candoli, Harry Edison and Jack Sheldon. On alto saxophone we hear Benny Carter, Herb Geller, Charlie Mariano and Art Pepper.

The tracks come from other composers and arrangers, such as Jimmy Giuffre, Johnny Mandel, Charlie Mariano and Lennie Niehaus. That gives the record a varied character. The line-up also differs from track to track: the rhythm section alternates between Lou Levy, Carl Perkins, Red Mitchell, Leroy Vinnegar, Shelly Manne and Mel Lewis. In the medley What's New?, each saxophonist gets a solo of his own. Thus Bill Perkins plays in What's New?, Pepper Adams in We'll Be Together Again and Walter Benton in Laura.
werk/quincy-jones-go-west-man.listen: Listen to the medley What's New / We'll Be Together Again / Time On My Hands / You Go to My Head / Laura and notice how the soloists take turns. Try to hear where one song passes into the next.

werk/quincy-jones-the-birth-of-a-band.text:
The Birth of a Band! was released in 1959 on Mercury and shows Quincy Jones as conductor and arranger for a big band. Many well-known soloists play on the record, including Zoot Sims, Clark Terry, Harry Edison and Phil Woods. Besides Jones, Nat Pierce, Al Cohn and Melba Liston also wrote arrangements. Liston also plays trombone herself.

The repertoire is a mixture of original work and well-known jazz pieces. Jones wrote the title track and, with Harry Arnold, A Change of Pace. There are also pieces by Bobby Timmons, Benny Golson, Lester Young and Sonny Stitt, and the old classic Tuxedo Junction. The tracks all last just two to four minutes. The reviewer Scott Yanow later called the record one of Jones's best jazz recordings.
werk/quincy-jones-the-birth-of-a-band.listen: Listen to Moanin' and notice how the whole band plays Bobby Timmons's bluesy melody together.

werk/quincy-jones-the-great-wide-world-o.text:
The Great Wide World of Quincy Jones came out in 1959 on Mercury. Jones stands as conductor in front of a big band including Art Farmer, Lee Morgan and Phil Woods. The arrangements come from four people: Ernie Wilkins, Al Cohn, Bill Potts and Ralph Burns. Jones himself wrote no tracks for this record.

The repertoire is broad. It includes jazz classics such as Lester Leaps In, Caravan, Cherokee and Air Mail Special, alongside a song by Irving Berlin and I Never Has Seen Snow by Harold Arlen and Truman Capote. Wilkins and Potts also wrote original pieces, such as Ghana and Eesom. Scott Yanow later described the record as a bop-oriented big band of the highest level.
werk/quincy-jones-the-great-wide-world-o.listen: Listen to Caravan and notice how the big band puts down this well-known theme by Juan Tizol and Duke Ellington together.

werk/quincy-jones-this-is-how-i-feel-abo.text:
In September 1956 Quincy Jones arranged and conducted three recording sessions for his first full album as a bandleader. Before that he had only taken part in the shared album Jazz Abroad from 1955. Each session had a different line-up, from a nonet to a fifteen-piece big band. The producer was Creed Taylor and the album was released in 1957 on ABC-Paramount.

Among those playing on the record are Charles Mingus, Art Farmer, Phil Woods, Lucky Thompson, Hank Jones, Paul Chambers, Milt Jackson, Art Pepper, Zoot Sims and Herbie Mann. The album thus shows how many top musicians the young arranger managed to gather around him. For the 1992 CD edition, bonus tracks from Go West, Man! were added and it appeared on the Impulse! label, which Taylor had later set up. The cover resembles the original, but carries the Impulse! logo.
werk/quincy-jones-this-is-how-i-feel-abo.listen: Listen to Walkin' and notice how the large ensemble of trumpets, trombones and saxophones plays together. Can you also hear the soloists rising above the arrangement?

werk/r-e-m-automatic-for-the-people.text:
Automatic for the People was released in October 1992. R.E.M. began writing while the previous record, Out of Time, was still high in the charts. Guitarist Peter Buck, bassist Mike Mills and drummer Bill Berry rehearsed without singer Michael Stipe and often switched instruments. As a result the sound became calmer, with more acoustic guitar and organ and fewer drums. The recording with producer Scott Litt followed in Woodstock, and on a few tracks there are strings by John Paul Jones.

The album reached number two in the United States and number one in the United Kingdom. Critics were mostly full of praise. Rolling Stone gave five stars. Six singles were released, including Drive, Man on the Moon and Everybody Hurts.
werk/r-e-m-automatic-for-the-people.listen: In Drive, listen to the strings that colour this sombre, quiet track. Notice how the vocals stay soft, even as the music grows bigger.

werk/r-e-m-document.text:
Document was released on 31 August 1987 on I.R.S. Records and was R.E.M.'s fifth album. It was the first record the band produced together with Scott Litt, a collaboration that would last for years. After Lifes Rich Pageant the vocals became more intelligible and the sound harder. The band also added new instruments: a dulcimer in King of Birds and a saxophone in Fireplace.

The One I Love became the first hit in the American top ten and the album reached number ten on the album chart. A Rolling Stone reviewer found it the band's best record up to then. Other critics wrote that with Document the group discovered the world outside itself, with more humour and more anger. The song It's the End of the World As We Know It (And I Feel Fine) was called by one reviewer the most sardonic apocalypse ever.
werk/r-e-m-document.listen: Listen to Fireplace and notice the saxophone. On this album the band used such extra instruments for the first time.

werk/r-e-m-fables-of-the-reconstruction.text:
Fables of the Reconstruction is R.E.M.'s third studio album and came out on 10 June 1985. After two albums with Don Dixon and Mitch Easter, the band wanted a different producer. Michael Stipe thought of Van Dyke Parks, but it became Joe Boyd, known for folk rock with, among others, Nick Drake and Fairport Convention. For the first time the band recorded outside the United States, at Livingston Studios in London. The weather was bad and Boyd's precise way of working, with hours of mixing, clashed with the band's spontaneous approach.

The sound is darker and murkier than on earlier records. The lyrics draw their themes and figures from the Gothic of the American South. There is more variety in instruments, with strings, brass and banjo. The reviews were positive and praised the folk elements in particular. Driver 8 has since become one of R.E.M.'s best-known and most covered early songs.
werk/r-e-m-fables-of-the-reconstruction.listen: Listen to Driver 8 and notice the guitar and the images from railway life in the lyrics.

werk/r-e-m-green.text:
Green is R.E.M.'s sixth studio album and was released on 8 November 1988 on Warner Bros. After Document the band had fulfilled its contract with I.R.S. They wanted to leave because the records were poorly distributed abroad. Warner offered complete creative freedom. The basic tracks were recorded between 24 May and 5 July 1988 at Ardent Studios in Memphis, with producer Scott Litt. Sessions followed in Bearsville, in New York State.

The group left the jangle pop of earlier records behind. Guitarist Peter Buck said they were writing major-key rock songs and switching instruments, and a mandolin, among other things, was added. Stipe asked his bandmates to stop writing typical songs. The album consequently sounds varied, with ironic pop songs such as Stand and Pop Song 89 and political themes in the lyrics and packaging. Green was a success with critics and public, and the band toured with it for eleven months.
werk/r-e-m-green.listen: Listen to Pop Song 89 and notice how cheerful and straightforward the track sounds, unlike the minor-key ballads of before.

werk/r-e-m-lifes-rich-pageant.text:
Lifes Rich Pageant is R.E.M.'s fourth studio album and was released on 28 July 1986 on I.R.S. Records. After a break from touring, the band wanted to get away from the murky, dense sound of the previous album. Producer Don Gehman had worked with John Mellencamp and got the job. In April and May 1986 they recorded at Mellencamp's Belmont Mall Studio in Indiana. Gehman had the band work with overdubs and layered arrangements, which was new to them.

The result sounds more direct and harder, with room for piano, organ, accordion and banjo. Michael Stipe's voice is much clearer in the mix. Cuyahoga is about a river in Ohio that caught fire several times because of pollution, and Fall on Me also has an environmental undertone. On the cover are drummer Bill Berry and two bison. The album was well received and was, up to then, the group's most successful record in the United States.
werk/r-e-m-lifes-rich-pageant.listen: Listen to Fall on Me and notice how clearly Michael Stipe's singing now comes forward in the mix.

werk/r-e-m-murmur.text:
R.E.M. began the debut album in December 1982, at first with producer Stephen Hague. That went wrong: he had the band play the same song countless times and added keyboards without permission. The label allowed a trial session with Mitch Easter and Don Dixon, and after that the band was allowed to record with them. In January and February 1983 it worked at Reflection Studios in Charlotte, North Carolina. The band wanted no guitar solos and no popular synthesizers, so that the album would sound timeless. Easter and Dixon intervened little.

The sound is rooted in folk rock, post-punk and garage rock. Michael Stipe's singing is mumbling and the lyrics are cryptic. Peter Buck plays jangling guitars and Mike Mills melodic bass lines. The album received glowing reviews for its unusual, atmospheric sound.
werk/r-e-m-murmur.listen: In Radio Free Europe, listen to Peter Buck's guitars and Michael Stipe's singing. Notice how hard it is to make out the words.

werk/r-e-m-reckoning.text:
Reckoning is R.E.M.'s second studio album and was released on 9 April 1984 on I.R.S. Records. After the acclaimed Murmur, the band wrote new songs at lightning speed, mostly in Mike Mills's living room in Athens, Georgia. Recording took place at Reflection Sound Studios in Charlotte, North Carolina, in December 1983 and January 1984. Mitch Easter and Don Dixon produced the record and wanted to capture the band's live sound. On a number of tracks they used binaural recording technique.

Singer Michael Stipe wrote darker lyrics than before, with water as a recurring image. The recording was hard going for him, because he was tired from touring. On 7 Chinese Bros. he sang so softly that Dixon could not hear him. He got hold of a gospel record and began reading out the sleeve notes, after which the vocals could be recorded properly. The album received glowing reviews.
werk/r-e-m-reckoning.listen: Listen to So. Central Rain (I'm Sorry) and notice how the guitars and the vocals sound together as if the band were simply playing live.

werk/radiohead-a-moon-shaped-pool.text:
In September 2014 Radiohead began work on this ninth album with producer Nigel Godrich, at their own studio in Oxfordshire. There was hardly a demo and no rehearsal period; the sound emerged during recording. Three weeks at the La Fabrique studio in France followed later. Godrich recorded on analogue tape, inspired by Motown and early David Bowie records. Jonny Greenwood wrote the strings and the choir, played by the London Contemporary Orchestra. Some tracks were years old: True Love Waits was first played back in 1995.

In Burn the Witch the strings play their instruments with plectrums instead of bows, which gives a percussive effect. For Daydreaming the band slowed the tape for the intro and the cellists detuned their cellos, for a growling sound. Many critics heard in the lyrics a response to the break-up of Thom Yorke and his wife. The album appeared on many year-end lists and received a Mercury Prize nomination.
werk/radiohead-a-moon-shaped-pool.listen: Listen to Burn the Witch and notice the strings: they sound sharp and rhythmic because the players use plectrums.

werk/radiohead-amnesiac.text:
Amnesiac came out on 30 May 2001 and arose from the same sessions as Kid A, between January 1999 and mid-2000 in Paris, Copenhagen and a new studio in Oxfordshire, with producer Nigel Godrich. Radiohead found the material too dense for a double album and split it in two. The music draws on electronics, twentieth-century classical music, jazz and krautrock. Thom Yorke treated his voice with AutoTune, and for Life in a Glasshouse the band of the trumpeter Humphrey Lyttelton played along.

Pyramid Song is a swinging ballad with piano and strings, inspired by a piece by Charles Mingus. Knives Out was called the most conventional song. The record topped the chart in England and was nominated for the Mercury Prize. Some critics found it less cohesive than Kid A, but the band saw it as an album in its own right. Rolling Stone, NME and Pitchfork later named Pyramid Song one of the best tracks of the decade.
werk/radiohead-amnesiac.listen: In Pyramid Song, listen to the piano and the strings and notice the swinging rhythm of this ballad.

werk/radiohead-hail-to-the-thief.text:
After Kid A and Amnesiac, which had been made with a great deal of studio experimentation, Radiohead wanted to work more spontaneously. In September 2002 the band went with producer Nigel Godrich to Ocean Way Recording in Los Angeles. There the group recorded most of it in two weeks, about a track a day, with an emphasis on live recording rather than overdubs. Singer Thom Yorke wrote lyrics under the impression of the election of George W. Bush and the war on terror. He combined political language with fairy tales and children's books.

The sound is more rock than on the two predecessors: live drums, guitar and piano, and less processed vocals. The opener 2 + 2 = 5 was a studio test and was finished in two hours. The album entered at number 1 in Great Britain and won a Grammy for best engineered album. The band members later found it too long and unfinished.
werk/radiohead-hail-to-the-thief.listen: Listen to 2 + 2 = 5 and notice how rock and electronics come together, with live-played drums and guitar and vocals that are less processed.

werk/radiohead-in-rainbows.text:
After the end of the EMI contract in 2003, Radiohead no longer had anything to deliver. The band began In Rainbows in 2005, at first without producer Nigel Godrich. The sessions went slowly, even a collaboration with Spike Stent produced nothing, and management even suggested stopping. A tour in 2006 helped to finish the new songs, and Godrich returned. Recording took place in country houses such as Halswell House and Tottenham House, at the Hospital Club in London and at their own studio in Oxfordshire. The lyrics are more personal and less political than before.

In October 2007 the album was released as a download for which fans set the price themselves. That was a first for a major band. Singles were Jigsaw Falling Into Place and Nude. The album won a Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album.
werk/radiohead-in-rainbows.listen: In Weird Fishes / Arpeggi, listen to the repeating guitar patterns and the vocals. Notice how the layers together form a single whole.
